claims.text: The cast Co-Cr-Fe-Ni starting alloy has coarse grains larger than 10 μm.
Cast Co-Cr-Fe-Ni alloys have limited ductility.
Homogenization at 1100°C for 2 h is suitable for the proposed alloy.
High-pressure torsion or cryogenic rolling will refine the Co-Cr-Fe-Ni alloy to a grain size below 50 nm.
Annealing at approximately 350°C for 1 h with 0.5–1.0 at.% C will retain grains below 50 nm without carbide precipitation.
Interstitial carbon segregates to grain boundaries, reduces interfacial energy, and suppresses grain growth or boundary motion.
Carbon lowers the stacking-fault energy of the FCC Co-Cr-Fe-Ni matrix.
A critical metastable stacking-fault-energy range enables FCC-to-HCP transformation and twinning, producing joint TRIP/TWIP behavior.
At 0.5–1.0 at.% C, the target alloy will form FCC and HCP solid solutions rather than carbides.
Adding Nb to CoCrFeNi can form a hard and brittle Co2Nb-type Laves phase.
Excluding Nb from the target composition avoids brittle Laves-phase formation.
Nanograin Hall–Petch strengthening combined with TRIP/TWIP will provide simultaneous high strength and high ductility.
The processed alloy will have yield strength above 1000 MPa, tensile strength above 1200 MPa, and elongation above 40%.
The processed alloy will contain equiaxed grains below 50 nm and approximately 20–30% HCP phase in an FCC matrix.
The cast baseline has a yield strength of approximately 300–400 MPa and elongation below 20%.
The cast baseline is either single-phase FCC or FCC+HCP depending on cooling rate.
Carbon contents above approximately 1.5 at.% cause M23C6 carbide formation in the target alloy.
Annealing above 500°C causes grain growth because carbon segregation no longer provides sufficient stabilization.
Excessively high stacking-fault energy produces single-phase FCC, whereas excessively low stacking-fault energy produces dominant HCP or brittle martensite.
The cited C-and-Mo-microalloyed Co-Cr-Fe-Ni study demonstrated carbide formation caused by high Mo and carbon contents.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis permits annealing at 300–400°C, while the conditions narrow this to 350–400°C and the intervention specifies only 350°C, leaving the status of 300–349°C inconsistent.

The boundary explicitly predicts failure above about 1.5 at.% C, yet carbide formation and ductility loss in the 2.0 at.% C specimen are called a falsification. That result would instead confirm the stated boundary condition and would not falsify the hypothesis within its proposed 0.5–1.0 at.% C range.
